idiom_name: poll loop: receive(timeout) / poll(max, idle) + idle backoff + batch cap + explicit ack
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the application a consumer object with one blocking call that waits at most an idle interval (receive(timeout), poll(duration), TryTake(item, timeout)) and returns nothing when the channel is empty, plus an immediate variant (receiveNoWait, try_recv) for callers that must not block; return at most a bounded batch per call so the amount of unprocessed work is a configured number. The loop around it owns four decisions - the idle interval and its backoff, the batch cap, the acknowledgement point (after processing, never at fetch time) and the shutdown signal that unblocks a waiting receive. Never spin without an idle policy, and never let the processing time of one batch exceed the transport's session or visibility timeout.
pitfalls: A receive that returns nothing is the idle case, not a fault: conflating empty with broken turns ordinary silence into an incident.
Acknowledging when the message is fetched rather than when it is handled loses in-flight work on a crash; acknowledging too late repeats it, so the handler must tolerate redelivery.
No shutdown path for a blocked receive: without an interruption mechanism (close, cancel token, wakeup) the consumer cannot stop while the channel is silent.
Wrong move: short-poll an idle SQS queue -> empty ReceiveMessage responses waste requests and cost -> instead use long polling with WaitTimeSeconds when the latency budget permits.
Wrong move: let Kafka batch processing exceed max.poll.interval.ms -> the consumer leaves its group and commits can fail -> instead bound max.poll.records or keep polling while work is processed.
Wrong move: claim PostgreSQL jobs without row locking -> competing workers can process the same row -> instead use FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED with a short acknowledgement transaction.
